Founded in 1907, Atalanta holds the record for having played the most Serie A seasons (65) without being based in a [[regions of Italy|regional]] capital and without having won the league title. Furthermore, the club holds the record for most promotions to Serie A,{{Efn|Thirteen times, the first in 1927–28 and the latest in 2010–11.}} and also that for the joint-most [[Serie B]] titles, alongside [[Genoa CFC|Genoa]]. Atalanta won the [[Coppa Italia]] in [[1962–63 Coppa Italia|1963]] and the [[UEFA Europa League]] in [[2023–24 UEFA Europa League|2024]].{{cite web |date=22 May 2024 |title=Atalanta win the 2023/24 UEFA Europa League: Meet the champions |url=https://www.uefa.com/uefaeuropaleague/news/0285-18dfede344d4-8ebefb1dffd1-1000--meet-the-2024-winners/ |access-date=22 May 2024 |publisher=[[UEFA]]}} The club qualified for the [[UEFA Champions League]] five times, reaching the quarter-finals in [[2019–20 UEFA Champions League|2020]], and participated in six seasons of the UEFA Europa League (previously known as the UEFA Cup).{{efn|This includes one appearance in the knockout stage after a group-stage elimination in the same season's Champions League.}} Atalanta also reached the semi-finals of the [[Cup Winners' Cup]] in [[1987–88 European Cup Winners' Cup|1988]], when it was competing in Serie B. This is still the joint-best performance ever by a non-first division club in a major [[UEFA]] competition.{{efn|Together with [[Cardiff City F.C.|Cardiff City]]}} The club plays its home games at the [[Stadio Atleti Azzurri d'Italia|New Balance Arena]] and its main kit colors are black and blue. Atalanta had a long-standing rivalry with nearby club [[Brescia Calcio]] until that team's dissolution in 2025; the rivalry continues with [[Brescia]]'s [[Phoenix club (sports)|phoenix club]], [[Union Brescia]]. The club is also famed for its [[Atalanta BC Youth Sector|youth academy]], which has produced several notable talents who have played in the top leagues of Europe.{{cite web|date=16 December 2016|title=How AC Milan and Others Have Benefitted from Atalanta's Production Line|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2682063-how-ac-milan-and-others-have-benefitted-from-atalantas-production-line|website=bleacherreport.com|access-date=31 January 2021}} ==History== {{Main|History of Atalanta BC}} ===Founding and establishment in Serie A (1907–1959)=== [[File:Atalanta 1930-present.png|thumb|right|upright=2|alt=Line graph depicting Atalanta's performances in the Italian league since 1930|Performances of Atalanta in the [[Italian football league system|Italian league]] since the first season of a unified Serie A]] Atalanta was founded on 17 October 1907 by students of the [[Liceo Classico Paolo Sarpi]] and was named after the [[Atalanta|female athlete of the same name]] from [[Greek mythology]].{{cite web|last=Di Santo|first=F. D.|date=8 March 2018|title=L'epidemia del "fùbal" a Bergamo: come nasce l'Atalanta|url=https://gazzettafannews.it/calcio/serie-a/atalanta/lepidemia-del-fubal-bergamo-come-nasce-latalanta/|access-date=14 December 2020|website=Gazzetta Fan News|language=it}} Though it immediately established a football sector,{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=23|loc=vol. 1}} it was not the first football association based in Bergamo: ''Football Club Bergamo'' was founded by [[Switzerland|Swiss]] emigrants in 1904{{cite web |url=https://www.diarionerazzurro.it/homepage/gli-inizi/ |title=Gli Inizi |website=mondoatalanta.it |language=it |access-date=11 January 2021}} and was absorbed into another club, ''Bergamasca'', in 1911. The [[Italian Football Federation]] did not recognize Atalanta until 1914, and in 1919 announced that it would only allow one club from Bergamo to compete in the [[Italian football league system|highest national league]] (then called the Prima Categoria). As Atalanta and Bergamasca were rivals and did not come to an agreement, admission to the Prima Categoria was decided by a playoff match; Atalanta won this match 2–0.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=33|loc=vol. 2}} A merger between the two clubs nevertheless occurred in 1920, forming the new club ''Atalanta Bergamasca di Ginnastica e Scherma 1907'' (shortened to ''Atalanta Bergamasca Calcio'') and establishing its black and blue (''nerazzurri'') colors.{{cite web|date=12 March 2017|title=Inter and Atalanta, two different Nerazzurri histories|url=https://www.inter.it/en/news/2017/03/12/inter-and-atalanta-two-different-nerazzurri-histories.html|access-date=14 December 2020|website=Inter.it – News|publisher=FC Internazionale Milano}}{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=38|loc=vol. 1}} Atalanta competed in the [[Seconda Divisione]], the second tier, during the early 1920s.{{cite web |url=https://www.footballhistory.org/club/atalanta.html |title=Atalanta BC club history |website=footballhistory.org |date=2019 |access-date=22 December 2020}} In the 1927–28 season, the club won its group and subsequently defeated [[U.S. Pistoiese 1921|Pistoiese]] in the playoffs to win promotion and its first second division league triumph.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=47|loc=vol. 2}} The club inaugurated its current home stadium in the Borgo Santa Caterina neighborhood in 1928,{{cite web|last=Salvatori|first=Thomas|date=2 June 2020|title=Temples of The Cult: Atalanta's Gewiss Stadium in Bergamo|url=https://cultofcalcio.com/temples-of-the-cult-atalanta-gewiss-stadium-bergamo/|access-date=15 December 2020|website=The Cult of Calcio}} and was admitted to [[Serie B]], the second tier of the restructured Italian league, in 1929.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=49|loc=vol. 2}} After almost a decade in Serie B, Atalanta achieved its first promotion to [[Serie A]] in 1937 under coach [[Ottavio Barbieri]],{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=70|loc=vol. 1}} though was [[promotion and relegation|relegated]] at the end of the season. The club returned to Serie A in 1940 as champion of [[1939–40 Serie B|Serie B]]. During the 1940s, Atalanta performed consistently in the top flight, though the national league was halted between 1943 and 1945 due to [[World War II]].{{cite web |url=https://www.goal.com/it/notizie/lo-spezia-e-lo-scudetto-dimenticato-quando-i-vigili-del/ttzxdv3pqk2q1lc5c64kb3yg9 |title=Lo Spezia e lo Scudetto dimenticato: quando i Vigili del Fuoco sconfissero il Grande Torino |date=27 September 2020 |last=Camedda |first=Paolo |website=Goal.com |language=it |access-date=24 July 2021}} Atalanta achieved a fifth-place finish in the [[1947–48 Serie A]] under coach Ivo Fiorentini, its highest league finish until 2017.{{cite web|last=Jackson|first=Marco|date=15 February 2017|title=Atalanta 1948: The Queen in Search of a Crown|url=https://forzaitalianfootball.com/2017/02/atalanta-1948-the-queen-in-search-of-a-crown/|access-date=15 December 2020|website=Forza Italian Football}}{{cite web |url=https://www.football-italia.net/SerieA/season/2016-17/Review/Club-by-Club/Atalanta |title=2016–17 Serie A Review – Atalanta |website=Football Italia |date=2017 |access-date=18 December 2020}} The club earned a reputation as the ''provinciale terribile'' (terrible provincial team) during this time as a result of its successes against well-known metropolitan teams such as the ''[[Grande Torino]]'', who won Serie A five times during the 1940s.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=95|loc=vol. 1}} Atalanta achieved mid-table finishes during much of the 1950s and remained in Serie A until 1958, when it was relegated due to accusations of [[match fixing]]. These accusations were found to be false a year later, after the club returned to Serie A by winning its second [[1958–59 Serie B|Serie B]] title.{{cite web |url=https://www.bergamonews.it/2011/08/10/atalanta-penalizzata-quella-volta-nel-1958/149660/ |title=Atalanta penalizzata, quella volta nel 1958 |date=10 August 2011 |website=bergamonews.it |language=it |access-date=31 December 2020}} ===Coppa Italia victory, decline, and reemergence in Europe (1959–1994)=== [[File:Atalanta BC - 1962-63 Coppa Italia - Angelo Domenghini and Piero Gardoni.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.6|alt=Atalanta players lifting the 1962–63 Coppa Italia|Atalanta players Angelo Domenghini and [[Piero Gardoni]] hoisting the 1962–63 Coppa Italia]] Atalanta won the [[Coppa Italia]] in [[1962–63 Coppa Italia|1963]], defeating [[Torino F.C.|Torino]] 3–1 in the [[1963 Coppa Italia Final|final]] thanks to a [[hat-trick]] by striker [[Angelo Domenghini]].{{cite web |url=https://www.ultimouomo.com/atalanta-coppa-italia-1963/ |title=Un sogno di 56 anni fa |language=it |last=Gaetani |first=Marco |date=14 May 2019 |website=ultimouomo.com |access-date=19 December 2020}} This was the senior team's first major trophy. During the early 1960s, the club made its debut in European competitions, among them the 1961–62 [[Mitropa Cup]], the Coppa dell'Amicizia, and the Coppa delle Alpi.{{cite web |url=https://primabergamo.it/viva-berghem/tutte-le-atalanta-della-storia-ci-han-portato-europa/ |title=Tuute le Atalanta della storia che ci han portato in Europa |publisher=Prima Bergamo |language=it |date=3 March 2017 |access-date=23 December 2020}} As domestic cup winners, the club qualified for the [[1963–64 European Cup Winners' Cup]], its first major [[UEFA]] competition, though was eliminated by Portuguese club [[Sporting CP]] in the first round. The club made a few more appearances in international (though not UEFA) cups during the 1960s, though was relegated in 1969 after a decade in the top flight.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|pp=161–163|loc=vol. 2}} During the 1970s, Atalanta experienced several movements between Serie A and Serie B, and was in the second tier for four consecutive seasons between 1973 and 1977.{{cite web |title=Storia |url=http://www.atalanta.it/site/societa/storia.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170817162046/http://www.atalanta.it/site/societa/storia.html|archive-date=17 August 2017 |access-date=15 August 2014 |website=atalanta.it |language=it}} Despite playing in Serie B at the time, the club developed several young players who moved on to historically bigger clubs and won the [[1982 FIFA World Cup]] with [[Italy national football team|Italy]].{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 262}}{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 281}} Several difficult seasons then saw Atalanta fall into Serie B in 1980 and [[Serie C1]] in 1981, when for the first time in its history, the club would play outside the top two tiers. This was a blow that revitalized the club, from which many changes in management followed.{{cite web |url=https://www.mediapolitika.com/2020/06/29/amarcord-un-anno-allinferno-lunica-serie-c-dellatalanta/ |title=Amarcord: un anno all'inferno, l'unica Serie C dell'Atalanta |last=Milan |first=Marco |date=29 June 2020 |language=it |access-date=17 December 2020}} Under new management,{{cite web |url=https://www.tuttoatalanta.com/auguri-a/cesare-bortolotti-l-imperatore-di-bergamo-2489 |title=Cesare Bortolotti, l'imperatore di Bergamo |date=29 September 2010 |publisher=tuttoatalanta.com |language=it |access-date=21 December 2020}} Atalanta comfortably won Group A of Serie C1 in 1982, returning to Serie B the next season and then to Serie A in 1984, where it would remain until 1987. Atalanta reached its second Coppa Italia final in [[1987 Coppa Italia Final|1987]], though lost 4–0 to [[S.S.C. Napoli|Napoli]] over [[two-legged tie|two legs]].{{cite web |url=https://www.calcioatalanta.it/2018/02/28/latalanta-le-volte-semifinale-andata/ |title=L'Atalanta e le altre volte in semifinale: ecco com'è andata |date=28 February 2018 |language=it |website=calcioatalanta.it |access-date=20 December 2020}} As Napoli also won Serie A that season and therefore qualified for the [[1987–88 European Cup|European Cup]], Atalanta qualified for its second [[1987–88 European Cup Winners' Cup|European Cup Winners' Cup]].{{cite web |url=https://thesefootballtimes.co/2018/11/15/the-speed-flair-and-drugs-of-claudio-caniggia-an-icon-who-lived-on-the-edge-of-greatness/ |title=The speed, flair and drugs of Claudio Caniggia, an icon who lived on the edge of greatness |website=thesefootballtimes.co |last=Cancian |first=Dan |date=15 November 2018 |access-date=21 December 2020}} This was a turning point for the club; [[Emiliano Mondonico]] was appointed as coach and the club would achieve promotion after only one season in Serie B. Mechelen]], who would eventually win the tournament.{{cite web |url=https://www.ultimouomo.com/i-pirati-europa-atalanta-coppa-delle-coppe-1987-88/ |title=I pirati d'Europa: quando l'Atalanta arrivò in (secondary) |- |2025–26 |[[New Balance]] |Lete / Snai Fun (secondary) |Zondacrypto |} ===Crest=== Atalanta has had five crests since its foundation, all of which depict some combination of the team's name (except between 1984 and 1993), colours, and (since 1963) the [[Greek mythology|Greek mythological]] athlete [[Atalanta]], from whom the club derives its name as well as its nickname ''La Dea''. [[File:Calcio di inizio Lecce Atalanta (cropped).jpg|thumb|200px|alt=Josip Iličić in an Atalanta away kit|[[Josip Iličić]] with Atalanta in 2020 (away kit, featuring the running girl in place of the club's crest)]] The club's first three crests were shields featuring the name Atalanta on top, coloured stripes on the left, and another symbolic representation on the right. The original crest dates back to 1907 and had the club's original black and white stripes alongside a blue patch. In 1963, after the club won the Coppa Italia, the crest was redesigned to feature black and blue stripes alongside a running girl representing Atalanta.{{cite web |url=https://thesefootballtimes.co/2020/03/09/behind-the-badge-copa90-the-story-of-atalantas-logo/ |title=Behind the badge: the story of Atalanta's logo |date=9 March 2020 |last=Munday |first=Billy |website=thesefootballtimes.co |access-date=22 December 2020}}{{cite web |url=https://radiogoal24.it/2020/04/16/oltre-lo-stemma-storia-e-spiegazione-del-logo-dellatalanta/ |title=Oltre lo stemma: storia e spiegazione del logo dell'Atalanta |date=16 April 2020 |last=Tabelli |first=Filippo |website=radiogoal24.it |language=it |access-date=4 August 2021}} The crest's colours and representation of Atalanta changed again in the 1970s, though followed the same basic shape as the 1963 version.{{cite web |url=https://1000logos.net/atalanta-logo/ |title=Atalanta logo and symbol, meaning, history, PNG |date=22 March 2021 |publisher=1000 Logos |access-date=4 August 2021}} In 1984, the crest underwent a major redesign: the club's name and the running girl's body were removed from the crest and its shape was changed from a shield to a circle. This "classic" crest featured a white [[silhouette]] of Atalanta's head on a black and blue background, enclosed in three [[concentric circle|concentric]] white, black, and golden yellow circles. Black, blue, and white were retained—as the club's colours—while yellow was added to represent the [[golden apple]]s, which according to mythology, [[Hippomenes]] tossed to Atalanta to distract her and defeat her in a [[footrace]]. The club's modern crest was designed in 1993. It incorporates the 1984 crest into its design, though tilts Atalanta's head and lacks the yellow circle. The name Atalanta and founding year 1907 were added respectively above and below the circle, which is enclosed in an [[ellipse]] featuring the same split black and blue background as the 1984 design. ==Stadium== {{Main|Stadio di Bergamo}} Atalanta has played at its current stadium, the 24,950-seater [[Stadio di Bergamo|New Balance Arena]] in the Borgo Santa Caterina neighborhood of Bergamo, since 1928. Prior to its opening, Atalanta played at several other grounds in Bergamo. Between its founding in 1907 and recognition by the FIGC in 1914, the club did not have a dedicated playing field and only played [[exhibition game|friendly matches]] in public spaces—the Piazza d'Armi and the Campo di Marte in Bergamo.{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=24|loc=vol. 1}} In 1914, Atalanta's first playing field was established on the Via Maglio del Lotto,{{cite web|last=Canavesi|first=Carlo|date=17 October 2019|title=112 anni di Atalanta: lo stadio di Bergamo|url=https://www.calcioatalanta.it/2019/10/17/112-anni-di-atalanta-lo-stadio-di-bergamo/|access-date=14 December 2020|website=calcioatalanta.it|language=it}} near the [[Seregno–Bergamo railway|Bergamo–Milan railway]]. It measured {{convert|90|by|45|m|ft|lk=on}} and had a seated capacity of 1,000 spectators.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 12}}{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=26|loc=vol. 1}}{{sfn|Corbani|2007|p=28|loc=vol. 1}} Due to financial hardship during [[World War I]], though, Atalanta was forced to sell the land containing its field, leaving it without a home ground. As a solution, [[Entrepreneurship|entrepreneur]] and [[Philanthropy|philanthropist]] Betty Ambiveri sold the Clementina field, an older venue in [[Seriate]] that hosted sporting events such as cycling, to the club.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 19}} The new field was inaugurated as the ''Atalanta Stadium'' and it hosted 14,000 spectators in its first match against ''La Dominante'' of [[Genoa C.F.C.|Genoa]]. With the growth of football in the 1920s, Atalanta needed a new stadium. The new stadium was constructed on Viale Margherita (now Viale Giulio Cesare), replacing a [[hippodrome]] that once occupied the site. Construction of the new stadium took one year; it opened in 1928 and cost 3.5 million [[Italian lira|lire]]. The stadium was named after [[fascism|fascist]] Mario Brumana; this was common naming practice in [[Fascist Italy (1922–1943)|fascist Italy]]. The Brumana stadium was much larger than the Clementina field, having a seated capacity of 12,000 spectators in two ''tribune'' (side stands) and a larger field measuring {{convert|110|by|70|m|ft}};{{cite web |url=https://www.atalanta.it/stadio/ |title=Stadio |publisher=Atalanta BC |website=atalanta.it |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}} it also featured a [[running track]], as it was planned to form part of a larger complex. On 1 November 1928, Atalanta played its first unofficial match at the stadium (a 4–2 victory against [[U.S. Triestina Calcio 1918|Triestina]]); the stadium was then officially inaugurated on 23 December 1928, when Atalanta defeated ''[[La Dominante Genova]]'' 2–0 in front of over 14,000 spectators. {{multiple image | align = right | direction = vertical | width = 240 | header = ''Curva Nord'' (north stand) of the Stadio Atleti Azzurri d'Italia | image1 = Trbuna Giulio Cesare.JPG | alt1 = View of the old Curva Nord from the Tribuna Giulio Cesare at the Bergamo stadium in 2012 | caption1 = Original concrete ''Curva Nord'' in 2012 | image2 = The Gewiss Stadium in 2020.jpg | alt2 = Pitchside view of the reconstructed Curva Nord in 2020 | caption2 = Reconstructed ''Curva Nord'' in 2020 }} After [[World War II]], the stadium was renamed the ''Stadio Comunale'' ("Municipal Stadium"), as [[Fall of the Fascist regime in Italy|fascism no longer existed in Italy]]. Expansion of the stadium began in the years following the war: the construction of a south stand (the ''[[Curva]] Sud'') began in 1949,{{cite news |url=https://www.ecodibergamo.it/stories/bergamo-citta/latalanta-compra-lo-stadio-di-bergamodagli-anni-20-al-futuro-foto-e-video_1236049_11/ |title=Lo stadio di Bergamo: dagli anni '20 al futuro |work=L'Eco di Bergamo |language=it |date=10 May 2017 |access-date=28 July 2021}} and a second stand at the north end (the ''Curva Nord'') followed during the 1960s, opening in 1971.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 336}} Later, in 1984, the running track was removed in order to expand the stadium's capacity upon Atalanta's return to Serie A after five years. The club's first match in the [[1984–85 Serie A]], a 1–1 draw against Inter, had an attendance of over 43,000 spectators, a record attendance for the Stadio Comunale.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 336}}{{cite web |url=https://www.bergamonews.it/2013/05/08/atalanta-juventusverso-i-24mila-spettatorisara-record-dincassi/174333/ |title=Atalanta–Juventus, verso i 24mila spettatori: sarà record d'incassi? |publisher=BergamoNews |date=8 May 2013 |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}}{{efn|The club's home attendance record was later broken in 2020, though that match was not played in Bergamo.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 336}}}} The ''Tribuna Giulio Cesare'' underwent modernization during the early 1990s, and the stadium was renamed the ''Stadio Atleti Azzurri d'Italia'' ("Blue Athletes of Italy") in 1994. In 1997, following the death of 22-year-old forward [[Federico Pisani]] in a car accident, the ''Curva Nord'' was nicknamed the ''Curva Pisani'' in his honor. Similarly, the ''Curva Sud'' was nicknamed the ''Curva Morosini'' in 2012 to posthumously honor 25-year-old youth academy player [[Piermario Morosini]],{{cite web |url=https://forzaitalianfootball.com/2012/04/atalanta-pay-tribute-to-piermario-morosini-by-renaming-the-curva-sud/ |title=Atalanta pay tribute to Piermario Morosini by renaming the Curva Sud |publisher=Forza Italian Football |date=17 April 2012}} who died following collapse on the field during a Serie B match between [[Delfino Pescara 1936|Pescara]] and [[A.S. Livorno|Livorno]].{{cite news|title=Italy footballer Morosini dies after collapse on pitch|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-europe-17714715|access-date=14 April 2012|newspaper=[[BBC News]]|date=14 April 2012}} In 2015, the stadium also expanded its side stands to offer pitchside views only several meters (feet) from the benches, a revolutionary feature of Italian stadiums at the time. On 10 May 2017, Atalanta announced the acquisition of the stadium from the ''[[comune]]'' for 8.6 million [[euro]]s, becoming one of only four Serie A clubs to own its home stadium.{{cite web|date=10 May 2017|title=Serie A side Atalanta agree deal to buy stadium|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/soccer-italy-att-stadium/soccer-serie-a-side-atalanta-agree-deal-to-buy-stadium-idUKL4N1IC4U9|access-date=17 December 2020|website=Reuters}}{{efn|The other three are Juventus, Sassuolo, and Udinese. All the remaining Serie A clubs play in municipally-owned stadiums.}} This acquisition allowed the club to authorize a renovation project for the stadium, for like many Italian stadiums, much of its structure and facilities were considered outdated. This renovation project was also necessary to upgrade the stadium to meet UEFA standards for hosting matches in UEFA competitions. Because the stadium was not ready at the time, Atalanta had to play its Europa League home matches at the [[Mapei Stadium]] in [[Reggio Emilia]] and its Champions League home matches in its debut season at [[San Siro]] in [[Milan]].{{cite web |url=https://football-italia.net/why-are-atalanta-playing-in-reggio-emilia/ |title=Why are Atalanta playing in Reggio Emilia? |author=Gaby |date=14 September 2017 |publisher=Football Italia |access-date=26 July 2021}}{{cite web |date=11 July 2019 |title=Atalanta to play at San Siro |url=https://www.football-italia.net/140653/atalanta-play-san-siro |access-date=13 July 2019 |publisher=Football Italia |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602102706/https://football-italia.net/atalanta-to-play-at-san-siro-2/ |archive-date=2 June 2021}} Following a sponsorship agreement with electronics company [[Gewiss (company)|Gewiss]] lasting at least until 2025, the stadium was renamed the Gewiss Stadium on 1 July 2019.{{cite web |url=https://sponsorship.sportbusiness.com/news/gewiss-takes-naming-rights-to-atalanta-stadium/ |title=Gewiss takes naming rights to Atalanta stadium |publisher=SportBusiness Sponsorship |date=1 May 2019 |access-date=30 July 2021}}{{cite news |url=https://www.atalanta.it/news/lo-stadio-di-bergamo-diventa-gewiss-stadium/ |title=Lo Stadio di Bergamo diventa Gewiss Stadium |website=atalanta.it |date=1 July 2019 |language=it}} On 6 October 2019, the renovated ''Curva Nord'' was inaugurated for Atalanta's home match against [[U.S. Lecce|Lecce]];{{Cite news |url=https://www.gazzetta.it/Calcio/Serie-A/Atalanta/06-10-2019/atalanta-lecce-serie-a-settima-giornata-bergamo-gewiss-stadium-35037555779.shtml |title=Atalanta, dolce ritorno! Entrate destinate a scopi sociali |date=25 May 2019 |publisher=Prima la Martesana |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}} On occasion, Atalanta's youth team also plays competitive matches at the Gewiss Stadium, most recently the [[Supercoppa Primavera]] in 2021.{{cite web |url=https://www.tuttoatalanta.com/primavera-1/supercoppa-primavera-al-gewiss-stadium-il-21-gennaio-56027 |title=Supercoppa Primavera al Gewiss Stadium il 21 gennaio |date=13 January 2021 |publisher=Tutto Atalanta |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}} ===Training ground=== Atalanta trains at the Centro Sportivo Bortolotti in {{ill|Zingonia|it}}, a complex first constructed during the community's development in the 1960s, before being acquired for Atalanta by president Achille Bortolotti and inaugurated in 1977.{{cite news |url=https://www.gazzetta.it/fuorigioco/08-03-2019/fuorigioco-casa-atalanta-zingonia-piccola-scampia-che-puo-rinascere-3202011835338.shtml |title=Fuorigioco a casa Atalanta: Zingonia, la "piccola Scampia" che può rinascere |date=11 March 2019 |work=La Gazzetta dello Sport |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}}{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 292}} The complex is used by the senior team for training and some friendlies, and the youth teams for training and home matches in youth competitions such as the [[Campionato Primavera 1]].{{cite news |url=https://bergamo.corriere.it/notizie/sport/21_luglio_11/atalanta-pronto-ritiro-zingonia-tutte-date-stagione-segnare-calendario-d2939638-e246-11eb-a101-49a08d5b8f51.shtml |title=Atalanta, pronto il ritiro a Zingonia. Tutte le date della stagione da segnare sul calendario |date=11 July 2021 |work=[[Corriere della Sera]] Bergamo |language=it |access-date=29 July 2021}}{{cite web |url=https://www.atalanta.it/en/news/primavera-first-day-in-zingonia/ |title=Primavera back to work in Zingonia |date=23 July 2021 |website=atalanta.it |access-date=29 July 2021}} Atalanta's renowned youth academy (''Scuola di Calcio''; see below) is also based in Zingonia, and has been a continuous point of investment for the club since its establishment.{{cite web |url=https://www.canofootball.com/articles/look-inside-atalantas-zingonia-academy-shaping-future-italian-football/ |title=A Look Inside: Atalanta's Zingonia Academy – Shaping The Future of Italian Football |website=canofootball.com |last=Clapham |first=Alex |date=14 November 2017 |access-date=29 July 2021}} ==Supporters== {{Quote box |quote = "Being a fan of Atalanta is part of the identity of Bergamo."{{cite news |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/football/54721132 |title=Atalanta: The underdog Champions League challengers with a "special" link to fans |publisher=BBC Sport |last=Kottis |first=Alexandros |date=3 November 2020 |access-date=6 August 2021}} |salign = |source = —Local newspaper ''[[L'Eco di Bergamo]]'' editor-in-chief Andrea Valesini (translated), 2020 | width = 300px | align = left }} {{as of|alt=According to a 2022 survey|2022}}, Atalanta is the 9th-most supported club in Italy, with an estimated 314,000 supporters.{{cite web |url=https://www.calcioefinanza.it/2022/08/08/classifica-tifosi-serie-a/ |title=Classifica tifosi Serie A: Juventus, Milan e Inter in vetta |publisher=Calcio e Finanza |date=8 August 2022 |language=it |access-date=9 August 2022}} Although Atalanta supporters are vastly outnumbered in Italy by fans of more titled clubs, the club's performances in recent years have drawn additional support, especially among younger generations. An increase of 43% was reported since 2019,{{cite news |title=Come tifa l'Italia |work=La Gazzetta dello Sport |date=17 August 2021 |page=18 |volume=125 |issue=193}}{{cite web |url=https://www.calcioefinanza.it/2020/09/16/classifica-tifosi-serie-a-2020-2021/ |title=Classifica tifosi Serie A 2020–2021: La Juve doppia Inter e Milan |publisher=Calcio e Finanza |last=Vivaldi |first=Stefano |date=16 September 2020 |language=it |access-date=6 August 2021}} peaking at about 350,000 in 2021, and decreasing by 10% after the club failed to qualify for European competitions in 2022. The club has also worked to grow its fanbase with the ''[[Neonati Atalantini]]'' initiative, implemented in 2010 by president Percassi, which gifts a free Atalanta replica shirt to all newborns born within the city limits of Bergamo. {{As of|2020}}, over 36,000 shirts have been distributed; similar programs have been more recently adopted by other Italian clubs as well.{{cite web |url=https://primabergamo.it/atalanta/progetto-neonati-atalantini-36mila-magliette-donate/ |title=Progetto "Neonati Atalantini", dal 2010 a oggi sono oltre 36mila le magliette donate |publisher=Prima Bergamo |last=Gennari |first=Fabio |date=12 February 2020 |language=it |access-date=6 August 2021}} Most of the club's fans reside within the [[Province of Bergamo]]; conversely, there are very strong ties between Atalanta and Bergamo's residents, who often gather together in close-knit groups in support of the club. Atalanta supporters (''[[tifosi]]'') are considered to be among the most passionate and loyal fans in Italy. Atalanta's [[Ultras]] gather mostly in the ''Curva Nord'' as the unified group Curva Nord 1907, formed from members of various Ultras groups under the leadership of Claudio "Il Bocia" Galimberti during the early 2000s.{{cite news |url=https://bergamo.corriere.it/bergamo/notizie/cronaca/12_novembre_16/bocia-ultra-atalanta-tifosi-inchiesta-galimberti-bergamo-2112730193632.shtml |title=Non va allo stadio ma il Bocia comanda ancora 400 ultrà |work=Corriere della Sera Bergamo |date=16 November 2012 |language=it |access-date=7 August 2021}} The ''Curva Nord'' Ultras were historically [[leftist]] but are now [[apolitical]]. A separate Ultras group, Forever Atalanta, gathers in the ''Curva Sud'', and is believed to still be leftist. Atalanta Ultras have a reputation as one of the most [[football hooliganism|violent]] Ultras groups in Italy, self-describing as "we hate everybody", and indeed having few friends and many strong rivalries.{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2014/jan/07/atalanta-serie-a-club-guide-ground-ultras-caniggia|title=Atalanta: Serie A alternative club guide |first=Richard |last=Hall |date=7 January 2014 |work=[[The Guardian]]}} The club and its Ultras have been punished on multiple occasions by the Italian Football League for violent or [[racist]] conduct.{{cite news Since 2002, Atalanta supporters have organized ''La Festa della Dea'' (the Festival of the Goddess), a multi-day festival to celebrate the club, almost every summer.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 557}} The celebration features music, local cuisine, and reverence for the club's history, management, and players (both former and current players).{{cite web|url=https://www.viverebergamo.it/festa-della-dea-orio-al-serio/ |title=Feast of the Goddess – Orio al Serio |date=11 July 2018 |website=viverebergamo.it |access-date=6 August 2021}}{{cite web |url=https://forzaitalianfootball.com/2012/04/the-brighter-side-of-italian-ultra-culture-and-their-fight-for-justice-in-calcio/ |title=The brighter side of Italian Ultra culture and their fight for justice in Calcio |date=27 April 2012 |last=Stupple |first=Clark |publisher=Forza Italian Football |access-date=10 August 2021}} Some contemporary players and coaches also have appeared at the celebration, most recently in 2018.{{cite web |url=https://www.bergamoesport.it/bentornata-festa-della-dea/ |title=Bentornata festa della Dea! |date=13 July 2018 |publisher=Bergamo e Sport |language=it |access-date=6 August 2021}} ===Friendships and rivalries=== Atalanta supporters have a long-standing friendship (''gemellaggio''; twinning) with supporters of [[Ternana Calcio|Ternana]]. The friendship between the two clubs' supporters is one of the oldest and strongest in Italy, persevering since the 1980s.{{cite news |url=https://corrieredellumbria.corr.it/news/umbria/26556716/bocia-stefano-galimberti-arrestato-terni-violato-daspo-ternana-bari-capo-ultras-atalanta.html |title=Il Bocia Stefano {{sic|nolink=y}} Galimberti arrestato a Terni, il capo ultras dell'Atalanta ha violato il Daspo per Ternana-Bari |date=16 March 2021 |work=[[Corriere dell'Umbria]] |language=it |access-date=10 August 2021 |archive-date=10 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810213124/https://corrieredellumbria.corr.it/news/umbria/26556716/bocia-stefano-galimberti-arrestato-terni-violato-daspo-ternana-bari-capo-ultras-atalanta.html |url-status=dead }}{{cite web |url=https://forzaitalianfootball.com/2015/08/war-and-peace-in-italian-football-the-ultras-gemellaggio-and-unexpected-friendships/ |title=War and Peace in Italian Football: The Ultras, Gemellaggio and Unexpected Friendships |last=Clancy |first=Conor |date=25 August 2015 |publisher=Forza Italian Football |access-date=10 August 2021}} Historically, both clubs' Ultras were brought together by shared political views, and they frequently visit the other club's ''Curva''.{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 518}} Supporters of the club also have a historical twinning with supporters of German club [[Eintracht Frankfurt]], a friendship similarly rooted in shared political views.{{cite news |url=https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/sport/football/football-news/who-german-football-hooligans-linked-13941978 |title=Who are the German 'football hooligans' linked with Concert Square carnage? |last=Prentice |first=David |date=23 November 2017 |work=[[Liverpool Echo]] |access-date=10 August 2021}} There are also friendly relations between fans of Atalanta and fans of [[Spezia Calcio|Spezia]] (since Atalanta's run in the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1988),{{cite web |url=https://sport.meteoweek.com/2021/03/10/atalanta-spezia-tifosi/ |title=Atalanta–Spezia: fra i tifosi l'amore è nato nel 1988 a causa del Malines |date=10 March 2021 |last=Mancini |first=Chiara |website=sport.meteoweek.com |language=it |access-date=10 August 2021}} [[Cosenza Calcio|Cosenza]], [[Cavese 1919|Cavese]], and Austrian club [[FC Wacker Innsbruck (2002)|Wacker Innsbruck]]. Atalanta supporters share their most intense {{ill|Atalanta BC–Brescia Calcio rivalry|lt=rivalry|it|Rivalità calcistica Atalanta-Brescia}} with supporters of [[province of Brescia|nearby]] club [[Brescia Calcio|Brescia]].{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/soccer/italian-serie-a/story/4001318/lombard-derby-between-atalanta-brescia-has-seen-it-all-the-crusadespigssherman-tanks |title=Lombard derby between Atalanta–Brescia has seen it all: the Crusades, pigs, Sherman tanks |date=29 November 2019 |publisher=ESPN |access-date=7 August 2021}} Meetings between the two clubs are sometimes known as the ''Derby Lombardo'' (Lombard Derby).{{cite web |url=https://www.webmagazine24.it/dominanti-affamati-e-superiori-il-derby-atalanta-brescia-piu-nerazzurro-di-sempre/ |title=Dominanti, affamati e superiori: il derby Atalanta-Brescia più "nerazzurro" di sempre |publisher=Web Magazine 24 |date=14 July 2020 |language=it |access-date=7 August 2021}}{{sfn|Losapio|2020|loc=section 942}} This rivalry has its roots in a historical feud between Bergamo and [[Brescia]] dating back to the [[Middle Ages]], beginning in 1126 when Bergamo expanded its territory by acquiring land put up for sale by Brescia; this led to a series of territorial disputes and armed conflicts between the two cities, among them the [[Battle of Cortenuova]] in 1237. Although armed conflict eventually ended and both cities were unified under the [[Kingdom of Italy]] in 1861, the cities' historical rivalry has defined the atmosphere of matches between Atalanta and Brescia for the entirety of the clubs' history. In 1993, tension between the clubs' supporters escalated further following a match (won 2–0 by Brescia) that was suspended three times due to violence in the stands, which resulted in over 20 spectators being hospitalized.[https://forzaitalianfootball.com/2019/11/war-pigs-and-rabbits-atalanta-and-brescia-meet-13-years-later/ War, Pigs and Rabbits: Atalanta and Brescia meet 13 years later], Conor Clancy, Forza Italian Football, 29 November 2019. }} The first person who was committed to set up the Atalanta youth teams was Giuseppe Ciatto. Every organisational aspect was dealt with and resolved by him, and he also took care to train the various teams. In 1949 Atalanta won the ''Campionato Ragazzi''. In the late 1950s former Atalanta player Luigi Tentorio (then Special Commissioner of the club) felt the need to start investing more systematically in youth: he decided to create a real youth sector, with its own independent structure from the first team. The youth sector was entrusted to Giuseppe Brolis, who created a partnership with various clubs in the [[Veneto]] and [[Friuli]] regions, building a network of scouts and young coaches. A crucial step in the history of the Bergamo youth sector took place in the early 1990s when the president [[Antonio Percassi]] implemented a new investment policy, especially at the youth level. He managed to convince [[Fermo Favini]] to leave [[Calcio Como|Como]] and entrusted him with the responsibility of the youth sector. The Atalanta youth system not only continued to increase the production of players for the first team, but began to win several honours in the most important national leagues. From 1991 to 2014, the various youth teams have won 17 national titles. Apart from successes at youth level, the Atalanta youth system is also one of the most highly regarded in Europe: according to a ranking by the study centre in Coverciano, Atalanta have the top youth system in Italy and the sixth in Europe, behind [[Real Madrid]], [[Barcelona]] and three French teams.
